title: We’ve Got a ‘Supersized’ El Niño on Our Hands
gist: The World Meteorological Organization issued its most certain forecast ever (near-100% likelihood) for a record-strength El Niño lasting through February 2027, which is already driving the hottest US summer on record, droughts in Sudan and Puerto Rico, and Pacific fishery disruption, with 2027 expected to be even hotter than 2026.

insights.claim: The World Meteorological Organization issued a 'nearly 100% likelihood' forecast that the current El Niño will last through February 2027 -- described as the most unequivocal statement in the history of WMO El Niño/La Niña updates.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Near-certain forecasting of an extreme weather event gives commodity, insurance, agriculture, and energy markets an unusually high-confidence window to price in disruption risk (crop yields, water stress, fishery output) through early 2027.
insights.quote: This is the first time that a WMO El Niño/La Niña Update has been so unequivocal.

insights.claim: This El Niño is forecast to be the strongest on record 'by a wide margin,' with impacts already being felt globally and expected to intensify in coming months.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A record-strength event implies outsized, possibly nonlinear economic disruption (agriculture, water infrastructure, insurance claims) beyond what historical El Niño base rates would predict.

insights.claim: El Niño typically raises global average temperature by roughly 0.1-0.2°C (0.2-0.4°F) via heat release into the atmosphere, but this year's event could produce an even bigger boost, making 2026 likely the hottest year on record and 2027 forecast to be even hotter due to lag in heat working through the climate system.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A two-year compounding heat cycle (2026 record heat, 2027 even hotter) gives a concrete forward timeline for climate-driven cost pressure on insurers, utilities, and agriculture -- not a one-off spike.

insights.claim: The UN separately warned that the world will likely cross 1.5°C of warming over the next few years, with this El Niño's extra warming compounding on top of underlying manmade climate change.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Breaching the 1.5°C threshold has direct implications for climate-policy triggers, carbon-pricing regimes, and physical-risk repricing across insurance and real-asset portfolios.
insights.quote: The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.

themes.theme: Early observed impacts and regional stress points

insights.claim: The US just experienced its hottest summer on record, with the heat 'almost certainly juiced up' by the developing El Niño even before the event reaches full strength.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Record US summer heat ahead of El Niño's peak implies utilities/grid operators and agriculture should expect further intensification, not a plateau, into 2027.

insights.claim: El Niño-driven drought is already exacerbating a multi-year hunger crisis in Sudan via low Nile water levels, while Puerto Rico has moved to water rationing due to dry conditions and infrastructure failures.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Concrete near-term humanitarian and infrastructure stress points (Sudan food security, Puerto Rico water/grid resilience) are early markers of where El Niño-linked capital and aid flows may be needed.

insights.claim: Eastern Pacific fisheries have been thrown into disarray by hotter-than-normal ocean waters linked to the El Niño.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Fishery disruption in the eastern Pacific is a direct commodity-supply signal for seafood markets and coastal economies dependent on those fisheries.

insights.claim: Climate scientist Daniel Swain says the scale of this El Niño's consequences may be poorly understood even by experts, calling it potentially the largest single climate event any living person has experienced (aside from long-term warming itself), and explicitly cautions against making specific predictions about outcomes given the uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A credentialed scientist flagging genuine uncertainty about second-order effects is itself a risk signal -- investors in weather-exposed sectors should widen tail-risk assumptions rather than rely on historical El Niño playbooks.
insights.quote: This is probably one of the larger, if not the largest, climate events...that anybody alive is potentially ever experiencing.
